video_title: [One Million AI Engineer Special] How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco
gist: Latent Space interview with Mihail Eric (Stanford CS146S adjunct, head of AI at Monaco) walking through his 10-week AI-native software engineering curriculum: harness internals, context engineering, skills, agent-ready codebases, code review as the new bottleneck, security, background agents and software factories. It also covers Monaco's build-vs-buy choices (Devin for review, in-house Monocoder) and its AI sales platform strategy; the '1 Million' in the title refers to the AI Engineer channel milestone, not the content.

insights.claim: Mihail Eric's Stanford CS146S 'The Modern Software Developer' course was substantially rewritten for its second run (fall 2026) because autonomous long-running coding agents advanced so much in one year.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Elite CS curricula now treat AI-native development as core practice, signalling how fast the developer workflow is shifting.
insights.quote: a big portion of the curriculum did change from last year

insights.claim: In a survey of Stanford sophomores and juniors in the course, essentially no student writes code by hand anymore; all use coding agents.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Coding-agent adoption among new entrants is near-universal, supporting durable seat demand for coding tools.
insights.quote: not a single person really types by by hand anymore

insights.claim: Entry-level engineers now face a much higher floor: a new graduate must perform close to a senior level rather than as a typical Google L3 to be valuable.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Junior hiring compresses; labor value shifts to engineers who can orchestrate agents, affecting tech labor markets and edtech.
insights.quote: it's not sufficient to just be like a you know an L3

insights.claim: swyx argues provocatively that most students are 'cooked' while a minority will become super valuable, raising the question of what happens outside elite schools like Stanford.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Implies bifurcated outcomes in the software labor market rather than uniform displacement.
insights.quote: most students are cooked some of them are going to be super valuable

insights.claim: Coding-agent vendors subsidize student usage: students have educational licenses (Claude, Cursor, likely Cognition) and the course secured extra credits from Factory, Cognition and OpenAI so students can 'token max'.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Vendors are competing for developer mindshare at the university pipeline level, a customer-acquisition cost worth tracking.

insights.claim: The course pairs students with AI-native open-source partners (e.g., Warp, Pi, Eve) so maintainers review their code, as a mentorship mechanism to prevent a widening gap between agent-adopting seniors and juniors.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: OSS projects double as recruiting funnels; dev-tool companies use education partnerships for talent and distribution.

insights.claim: Hosts say building benchmarks and evals is the best way for students to get hired at frontier labs and agent labs, and that there is also money to be made turning benchmarks into businesses; SWE-bench started as an undergrad project at Princeton.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Eval/benchmark companies are a live startup category with strong lab demand.
insights.quote: make benchmarks and evals. Uh this will get you uh a good one going to get you in the door of every frontier lab

insights.claim: Ambition expectations have risen: turning a photo of sketches into an app is no longer impressive, whereas projects like a Cursor engineer building a browser with agents are what stand out and get recruited.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: The bar for differentiated software output is rising fast as agent capability commoditizes simple apps.
insights.quote: snapping a photo and turning into an app is not that ambitious in in the this day and age

insights.claim: swyx says he does not want to hire anyone who hasn't gone through 'AI psychosis' (over-elaborate agent tinkering) and come out the other side, because paying an employee to go through it costs salary and tokens with nothing delivered.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Token spend without output is a real cost line; productivity from agents is not automatic and depends on disciplined users.
insights.quote: I do not want to hire anyone who hasn't been through psychosis and come out the other end

insights.claim: A functional coding agent's core agentic loop can be built in about 200 lines of code using only introductory-algorithms-level knowledge; the rest is bells and whistles like subagents and MCP.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: The basic harness is commoditized; durable moats in coding agents must come from models, distribution or deep tooling, not the loop itself.
insights.quote: it doesn't require more than 200 lines

insights.claim: Claude Code's early popularity came from simplicity: fewer, more powerful 'Swiss Army knife' tools like Bash rather than many specialized tools.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Product simplicity, not feature count, drove category leadership in coding agents.
insights.quote: let's fewer tools do more

insights.claim: Claude Code's system prompt (around 20,000 tokens, the longest among coding agents) has see-sawed in size, and instructions such as how to use git have been removed because those behaviors are now baked into model weights.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Capability migrating from harness to model weights favors model labs over thin harness wrappers.
insights.quote: cloud code has the longest system prompt of all the coding agents. Something like 20,000 tokens.

insights.claim: Boris (Claude Code creator) explicitly built for where models would be six months out, and Opus model gains were a key reason the course curriculum changed so much.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Building ahead of model capability was validated; products positioned for the next model generation can leapfrog incumbents.
insights.quote: built for where the model is going to be 6 months from now

insights.claim: Very few engineers in industry progress beyond vanilla prompting; scaling agents to codebases with millions of lines requires a structured research-proposal-plan-implement-test workflow (similar to Dex's RPI) with a human choosing among proposals.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Enterprise value of coding agents depends on workflow maturity, implying a services/training gap and a long adoption runway.
insights.quote: the very few people in industry even progress beyond like just vanilla prompting

insights.claim: Multi-agent context management remains unsolved art: giving subagents too little context fails, while giving more context makes them overfit to stray one-off comments.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Orchestration and context tooling is an open product opportunity rather than a solved layer.

insights.claim: Mihail remains pro-MCP, viewing it as an established standard that will persist despite a period of hate.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: MCP-related infrastructure (portals, gateways) is a durable layer to watch.
insights.quote: I'm still pro MCP

insights.claim: Skills are prone to sloppiness: default skill-creation tools produce bloated skills, badly written triggers fire unexpectedly, and some practitioners prune skills every few weeks; swyx claims some smart people at Anthropic privately want skills to die.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: The skills/markdown-file paradigm may be transitional, a risk for businesses built around skill marketplaces.
insights.quote: There are very smart people at over in anthropic that want skills to die.

insights.claim: A more durable use of skills is codifying org-level best practices (API conventions, service boundaries) that code-review agents like Devin enforce, rather than ad hoc procedures.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Org-knowledge encoding is where agent tooling gets sticky inside enterprises.

insights.claim: Anthropic's 'dynamic workflows' pattern, writing a harness on demand for a task and running it as a subagent, is gaining traction, and Monaco has built its own version for go-to-market use cases.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Meta-harness patterns shift value toward orchestration layers.

themes.theme: Code review bottleneck and agent-ready codebases

insights.claim: Code review has become the main bottleneck in AI-native development because generation velocity is so high an engineer could put up 30+ PRs a day, while review capacity has not grown in line with merges.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: AI code-review and verification tools address the binding constraint, making them a high-value category.
insights.quote: you could in theory like put up 30 plus PRs a day

insights.claim: The emerging middle ground is auto-approving a class of PRs when agent-readiness and verifiability are designed in, while humans review the rest, possibly at the spec level rather than line by line.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Auto-approval readiness becomes a buying criterion and a feature race among review vendors.

insights.claim: Agent-ready codebases (verifiability, structure, docs, service boundaries) are the prerequisite for multi-agent parallelism, background agents and software factories; Factory's readiness report is a standout tool here.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Firms with agent-ready codebases will capture outsized productivity; readiness tooling is a wedge product.

insights.claim: At enterprise scale, the real blockers to AI-native development are often foundational DevOps/CI-CD issues such as backed-up merge queues and slow app stand-up, not a lack of more agents.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI-coding ROI may be capped by legacy infra, benefiting CI/CD and platform vendors.
insights.quote: the answer is not even always just more agents

insights.claim: Even frontier software-factory builders like Warp and Factory claim only about 30-some percent of contributions as fully agent-driven.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Fully autonomous 'dark factory' claims should be discounted; the transition is gradual.
insights.quote: even they only claim like 30 some% of even that

insights.claim: Humans remain the chokepoints in software factories at intent (specs) and review, and the review bottleneck will loosen before the intent bottleneck does.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Spec/intent tooling may be the longer-lived human-in-loop product category.

insights.claim: swyx says keeping a whole-codebase spec current is unsolved and models are bad at it; he is working on a git replacement ('program database') capturing traces, specs, intent and skills with high concurrency, and predicts Linear, holding the tasks, is likely the winner here.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Version-control and source-of-truth layers for agent work are being contested; Linear is positioned to expand into coding agents.
insights.quote: probably not me linear

insights.claim: Mihail predicts many B2B software companies that collect user or product insight will evolve into coding-agent companies that close the loop by fixing the product, citing Linear, Amplitude, Decagon and Sierra as possibilities.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Expect adjacent SaaS players to enter coding agents, intensifying competition and expanding TAM.
insights.quote: a lot of companies are going to evolve into some version of a coding agent company

insights.claim: Monaco follows 'buy to learn, build to keep': it built internally when no mature vendor existed, but still buys Devin for code review.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Vendors win only when clearly mature; otherwise AI-native firms build in-house, limiting TAM for immature tools.
insights.quote: you buy to learn and you build to keep

insights.claim: A year-plus-ago survey of AI code review tools (CodeRabbit, Graphite, Ellipsis and others) found none crossed the 'immediately useful' threshold, but on retry Devin spread organically as engineers asked to be added.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Bottoms-up organic adoption is a strong signal of product-market fit for Cognition's Devin Review.
insights.quote: people were just like, "Hey, Devon is like good. Like can can you like add me to this?"

insights.claim: Monaco built its own background-agent platform, 'Monocoder', on the Coder platform (coder.com), similar to Ramp Inspect, Stripe Minions and Spotify's internal systems.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Large adopters are standardizing on internal background-agent infra; Coder benefits as an underlying environment layer.

insights.claim: AI SRE vendors (e.g., Resolve) deliver the most value at enterprises with sprawling service dependencies and Kubernetes/Helm infrastructure like Ford or Walmart, while smaller companies can roll their own.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: AI SRE is an enterprise-skewed market; mid-market demand is weaker.

insights.claim: Every agent product is a coding agent under the hood, including consumer-facing ones such as a Cursor-built consumer bot and Claude in the app; swyx runs all his SEO/AEO work in Codex with a codebase.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Coding agents are the general substrate of agentic products, expanding their addressable market beyond developers.
insights.quote: They're all coding agents under the hood.

insights.claim: MCP portals are an unproven business and will fold into LLM gateways, auth and billing as the same 'god box' layer, though OpenRouter's success shows a focused routing-only point solution can win.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Standalone MCP-portal startups face consolidation risk; gateways that bundle governance may win.
insights.quote: MCP portals is a unproven business

insights.claim: Enterprise consolidation of gateways and MCP portals is held back more by org politics (separate teams owning stack parts) than by software design.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Conway's-law dynamics slow platform consolidation, keeping room for point vendors.

insights.claim: Platform engineering, owning cloud, DevX, security and ops, is described as an increasingly important future role.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Platform teams are the key buyers of AI dev infrastructure.

insights.claim: Supply-chain risk is central to AI-era security: pin dependencies and avoid blind npm install; the most secure codebase may have no dependencies, though swyx counters that open source gains security from many eyes.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Supply-chain security tooling (e.g., Socket) gains relevance as AI-generated code and dependency attacks grow.

insights.claim: A VC told swyx that Wiz and Socket are the only security companies in the last five years that have worked from a venture-returns perspective.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Security venture returns are concentrated; incidents drive sales cycles.
insights.quote: Apparently whiz and socket the only security companies in the last 5 years that have worked.

insights.claim: swyx doubts that models will fix all security, arguing they may introduce new kinds of bugs and that staged release of cyber models to ~100 blessed organizations creates new attack vectors.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Model-driven security is unproven; demand for independent scanning and review persists.

insights.claim: Security-critical code areas (data storage, billing, auth) should not be vibe coded, while elsewhere agents can run freely.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Risk-tiered review policies will shape how enterprises deploy autonomous coding.
insights.quote: those are basically don't vip code and then everything else go nuts

insights.claim: Mihail believes most OSS repos will become agent-run software factories, citing Warp running its open-source terminal as one, leaving it unclear whether such codebases become more or less vulnerable.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Shifting OSS maintenance to agents changes supply-chain risk profiles.
insights.quote: most OSS repos if not all of them will just become soft for factories

insights.claim: Monaco is a Series B, SF-based all-in-one AI-native sales platform that targets seed-to-Series A startups, growing with them up-market instead of displacing Salesforce in enterprises.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Classic land-with-startups strategy to unbundle Salesforce from below.
insights.quote: It's much harder to pull someone away from from Salesforce

insights.claim: Monaco's most valuable system is its 'world database' of enriched companies, accounts and contacts, using vendors Parallel and Exa plus in-house enrichment, with timing signals like job changes triggering outreach.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Proprietary data and timing signals, not models, are the moat in AI GTM tools; Parallel and Exa gain enterprise traction.

insights.claim: Monaco pairs its platform with forward-deployed account executives, ex-Brex GTM people, who onboard customers and build their agentic workflows, arguing that without this domain expertise the product would be commoditized.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Vertical AI defensibility increasingly relies on human forward-deployed teams and domain codification.

insights.claim: Vertical AI companies start on frontier models but, as cost matters, move to post-training open-weight models with RL environments, referencing the debate over Harvey's margins; Monaco is in that phase now.
insights.speaker: Mihail Eric
insights.so_what: Margin pressure pushes agent labs toward own models, a negative for frontier API revenue concentration in vertical apps.
insights.quote: the plus 50% to minus 50% margin kind of question

insights.claim: Monaco's plane-banner ads cost about $6,000 a day, cheaper than a billboard, and work as an icebreaker even if they don't explain the product; Monaco also won a lawsuit over buying the monaco.com domain.
insights.speaker: swyx (host)
insights.so_what: Cheap guerrilla brand marketing is a growth tactic in the crowded AI SaaS market.
insights.quote: $6,000 a day
